## 6. Your four skills: gap analysis

Scored on the five axes you asked for. **Verdict** is your position relative to the best of the two reference repos.

### 6.1 `to-jira-issues` — 138 lines + 143 reference lines

**What's strong.** The Jira mechanics are genuinely hard-won and better than anything in either reference repo: the two-call `createJiraIssue` (markdown) → `editJiraIssue` (ADF `taskList`) sequence with the field-discovery fallback, the write guardrail ("never create unless explicitly asked"), the mandatory change-comment on every evolve with `Originally requested by`, "never close or modify a parent issue", and the business-content-above-the-divider structure with an Estimation Criteria blast-radius sentence instead of story points. The `references/slicing.md` tracer-bullet + expand→migrate→contract methodology is a faithful port of Matt's and is correct.

| Axis                       | Assessment                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Token efficiency**       | **Weak.** The "Default instructions (always apply)" block is ~1,400 words of MUST-level prose that loads on *every* invocation, including a read-only "summarise this ticket" case. Roughly half of it is connector mechanics (the ADF payload shape, field discovery, call ordering) that only the create/evolve paths reach. Per Matt's branching test, that is textbook disclosed-reference material: inline what every branch needs, push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. The description is also 90 words and permanently resident.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Process maturity**       | **Weak — the biggest gap in your base.** There is no elicitation stage at all. Stage 1 resolves a source, Stage 2 explores code, Stage 3 classifies, Stage 5 drafts. Between "here's a requirement" and "here's a drafted issue" nothing interrogates *you*. Both reference repos treat this as the highest-leverage step in the whole system, for the same stated reason — "no-one knows exactly what they want." There is also no spec artifact: the Jira issue is the source of truth, so downstream review and implementation have no higher authority to argue from when the ticket and the code disagree. Superpowers' whole loop rests on "the spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument"; you have only the argument.                                                                                                     |
| **Process flexibility**    | **Mixed.** Three modes (single / breakdown / evolve) is good, and the cap-override grammar (state a number / say "no cap" / default 20) is a nice touch. But the three modes are welded into one skill, so the 138-line body plus both references is the entry cost for all of them. Matt gets more flexibility from *less* text by splitting into `grilling` → `to-spec` → `to-tickets`, each independently invocable and independently composable.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **General approach**       | **Two structural issues.** (a) **Sizing uses the wrong primitive.** A ≤15/hard-20 file cap is mechanical and gameable — a 20-file *horizontal* slice passes the cap. Both reference repos size by *semantics*: "demoable or verifiable on its own", "fits one fresh context window", "the smallest unit worth a fresh reviewer's gate". Keep the file count as a *sanity check*, not the rule. (b) **No per-ticket interface contract.** Superpowers' measured finding is that cross-task ambiguity is what causes review loops, and review-loop count is their biggest cost variance. For your stack this is acute: the Avro schema name, the topic, the `Event-Type`/`Schema-Name`/`Correlation-Id`/`Causation-ID` headers, the DTO shape, the repository group — every one of those is a cross-ticket contract that currently lives nowhere. |
| **Addresses your naivety** | **Partly.** The domain-vocabulary instinct in Stage 2.2 is exactly right — and then it's thrown away. Every session re-derives `RequestStatus`, `DispatchStatus`, `CommunicationSent`/`CommunicationFailed`, `template_identifier` from the codebase. `CONTEXT.md` caches that once and pays back every session, in every skill, forever. Separately, the prose is heavily negation-driven (~25 instances of never/must not/do not) — per Matt's writing-for-agents, prohibition drags the forbidden behaviour into context and half-reads as an instruction to do it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Verdict:** best-in-class Jira *mechanics*, immature *process*. It is doing the job of four skills and missing the one that matters most.

---

### 6.2 `implement-issue` — 52 lines

**What's strong.** Your token instincts are already ahead of Matt's `implement` (7 lines) on several concrete points: knowledge-graph-before-source-files, targeted line-range reads instead of full files, the explicit "never ask a sub-agent for full file contents", "one pass, not two", description-and-AC-only Jira fetching with a sparseness threshold for comments, and filtered `mvn` output with an unfiltered re-run only for the failing class. Those are real, correct optimisations that neither reference repo states this precisely. "The user must always see the full list of findings and how each one was addressed" and the AC honesty requirement are both good governance.

| Axis                       | Assessment                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Token efficiency**       | **Good tactics, wrong strategy.** Every optimisation you have is about reading *less into one context window*. The strategy both reference repos converged on is *not using one context window at all*: dispatch a fresh subagent per task, hand it a brief file path, get back <15 lines. Superpowers' own cost breakdown puts controller resident context at the top of the bill precisely because everything accumulates and is re-read on every subsequent turn. You also never specify a model — so every operation, including mechanical transcription, runs on the session model. Superpowers is explicit that this "silently defeats" tiering, and their guidance is nuanced enough to be trustworthy (mid-tier as the *floor* because turn count beats token price).                                                                                                         |
| **Process maturity**       | **Weak.** Missing, in rough order of cost: **(1) no plan artifact** — ticket goes straight to code, so nothing survives compaction and there is no resume point; **(2) no ledger** — after a compaction mid-issue you cannot tell which parts are done except by reading the diff; **(3) no worktree or branch isolation** — "commit your work to the current branch" is the entire branch policy, with no clean-baseline verification and no guard against implementing on `main`; **(4) no verification gate** — "full test suite once at the end" is a *habit*, not a gate; nothing forbids "should be passing now"; **(5) no escalation contract** — no DONE / DONE_WITH_CONCERNS / BLOCKED / NEEDS_CONTEXT vocabulary, and nothing tells the agent it is allowed to say "this is too hard for me"; **(6) no debugging route** — when a test fails, the skill has nothing to say. |
| **Process flexibility**    | **Weak.** One path, one issue, one context. No branch for "this issue is actually three tickets", no branch for spike vs bounded vs architectural (Superpowers' classification), no batching of same-shape work, no parallelism across independent tickets (Matt's `implement-spec` beta does exactly this with a frontier + worktrees).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **General approach**       | **One decision worth revisiting.** "Run the review exactly once. Do not re-run the review — the test suite is the correctness safety net, not a second review pass." The instinct (avoid unbounded review churn) is right, and both reference repos agree that *broad* re-review is waste. But the answer they landed on is better than zero: a **scoped** re-review over *only the fix diff*, which is cheap, and which verdicts each finding ADDRESSED / NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage introduced by the fixes. "The fix was small, skip the re-review" is literally a row in Superpowers' rationalization table, with the reason given: unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Bound the loop (5 rounds, escalate the model at round 4, adjudicate at the cap) rather than removing it.                                                                                 |
| **Addresses your naivety** | **This skill is where your ceiling is.** Everything runs in your session, on your model, in one window, with no durable state. It works for a 15-file ticket and degrades sharply beyond that — which is exactly why `to-jira-issues` needs a 20-file cap. The cap is a symptom: you sized your *tickets* around the limits of your *executor*. Fix the executor and the cap can relax to something semantic.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Verdict:** the best token *tactics* of the three repos, wrapped around the least mature *process*. Highest-leverage skill to rebuild.

---

### 6.3 `code-review` — 105 lines + 25 reference lines

**What's strong.** This is your best-engineered skill, and in several respects it improves on Matt's original that it was forked from:

- Discovers `*-standards` skills **by naming convention** rather than hardcoding, with the stated reason (java-21 today, java-25 tomorrow).
- Resolves the skills base from the absolute path of the SKILL.md itself, and searches *three* roots, because the CWD is the service repo not the skills base — a real bug Matt's version would hit.
- **Fails loudly on zero matches** and refuses to present a smell-baseline-only result as a Standards review. That is precisely the silent-degradation class your own audit process exists to catch, closed pre-emptively.
- Deduplicates by `name:` with repo-local precedence, matching the `CODING_STANDARDS.md` override rule.
- Uses `git diff --stat` to *select* which reference files the sub-agent reads (`*Controller*` changes → `13-controllers.md`) instead of reading all 76 of them.
- Passes **paths and commands, never contents** — stated with the reason ("avoids paying for the same content in both your context and theirs").
- Handles the classification-scheme mismatch case ("if a skill's scheme isn't MUST/SHOULD/…, use whatever it documents").

| Axis                       | Assessment                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Token efficiency**       | **Good, with one clean win left.** Both sub-agents are told to run `git diff <fp>...HEAD` themselves — so the diff is generated twice and lives in two contexts. Superpowers' `review-package` script writes one file (`# Commits` + `## Files changed` + `git diff -U10`) and hands both reviewers the path; the diff never enters the controller's context and is generated once. Two more: neither sub-agent is given a **model** (so both inherit the session model — the most expensive), and the 400-word cap is applied to both axes regardless of diff size.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Process maturity**       | **Two axes, missing the third.** Standards and Spec both *presuppose the code works*. Neither asks "is there a bug." Superpowers' reviewer covers five families — plan alignment, code quality, architecture, **testing** (do the tests verify real behaviour or mock behaviour), and **production readiness** (migration strategy, backward compatibility). For a Kafka + outbox + JPA microservice, that omission is expensive: Avro schema compatibility, consumer idempotency, `writerTransactionManager` boundaries vs outbox publication, DLQ handling, header/MDC propagation — none of these are a "standards violation" or a "spec gap", and all of them are where the production incidents come from. There is also **no severity taxonomy and no verdict** — findings are aggregated verbatim with "the worst issue within each axis", so `implement-issue` downstream has no way to know what *blocks*. And no adversarial verification step, so plausible-but-wrong findings ship as findings. |
| **Process flexibility**    | **Mixed.** Read-only by construction, with the reason stated (write guardrail consistency with `to-jira-issues`). That's defensible, but it means there's no `--comment` or `--fix` mode, and `pr-comment-addresser` exists as a separate skill — so the seam between "review" and "act on review" is unbridged. No effort dial either (the harness's own `/code-review` has low→max levels trading finding count against confidence).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **General approach**       | **Right, and the axis separation is a genuinely good idea** that Superpowers lacks — "don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent" is correct and worth keeping. The gap is that two axes were never meant to be the whole review.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Addresses your naivety** | **Yes, mostly.** This skill shows you already understand context economy and silent-failure modes. What's missing is the reviewer-trust dimension Superpowers learned the hard way: reviewers are not told to treat the implementer's claims as unverified, nor that "a stated rationale never downgrades a finding's severity" (the implementer saying "left it per YAGNI" is grading its own work), nor "do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer."                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Verdict:** structurally the strongest of your four. Needs a correctness axis, a severity taxonomy with a verdict, one review-package file, and explicit models.

---

### 6.4 `tdd-by-example` — 219 lines + 97 reference lines

**What's strong.** On *coverage* this is the best TDD skill of the three, and by a wide margin. It has:

- Beck's four moves to green, correctly framed as unranked and mixable (Fake It / Obvious Implementation / Triangulate / Property-Based).
- **Outside-In / double loop** (Freeman & Pryce) with an explicit "when to use vs classical" test — *neither reference repo has this*, and it is the correct default for a Spring Boot vertical slice (controller → service → repository).
- **Characterization testing** (Feathers) for brownfield work, including the counter-intuitive-but-correct "write the assertion *after* seeing the output; this is intentional, not cheating" — *neither reference repo has this*, and for a legacy credit-domain service it is the bridge that makes TDD applicable at all.
- **Test Desiderata** (all 12), correctly framed as tensioning against each other rather than as a checklist to max out.
- The test-list distinction that actually explains itself: "a checklist item costs you nothing to have been wrong about; a written test function you haven't run yet is a claim about behaviour you haven't checked."
- The escape-hatch signal is genuinely sharp: "you're about to write a conditional, a loop with more than one branch, or any step that reconciles/combines/transforms data from more than one source" — plus the right reason (silent wrongness, not crashing, is the risk).

| Axis                       | Assessment                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Token efficiency**       | **Weak.** 219 lines, loaded inside `implement-issue`'s context for every issue. The cycle itself — two underlying rules, four moves, refactor-only-on-green — is ~40 lines. Test Desiderata (20 lines), the worked Roman-numeral example (28 lines), outside-in (22 lines), and characterization (20 lines) are all *branch-specific* reference: only some runs reach them. That is exactly the progressive-disclosure test. Also: the escape-hatch section (16 lines) is longer and more prominent than the enforcement, which inverts the emphasis.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Process maturity**       | **Weakest enforcement of the three.** Yours is a *guide*; Superpowers' is a *law*. Compare: yours says "Don't write a line of production code without a failing test that demands it." Theirs says the same thing, then adds "Wrote code first? **Delete it.** Don't keep it as reference, don't adapt it, don't look at it. Delete means delete" — plus 10 rationalization rows, 13 red flags all resolving to "start over", and a pristine-output requirement. Also missing: a **RED-evidence contract**. Superpowers' implementer template *requires* the command run, the failing output, and why the failure was expected. Yours says "show the user the relevant lines" — softer, and unverifiable by any downstream reviewer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Process flexibility**    | **Good** — arguably the most flexible of the three (classical vs outside-in vs characterization, four moves, a properly-reasoned escape hatch). The risk is the flip side: a permissive skill with weak enforcement is a skill that gets talked out of the cycle.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **General approach**       | **Two missing ideas, both from Matt, both high-value for your stack.** (a) **Seam discipline**: "test only at pre-agreed seams, confirmed with the user before any test is written; prefer existing seams; use the highest seam possible; the fewer seams the better, ideally one." You have *four* Java testing skills — `unit-testing`, `db-core-jpa-integration-tests`, `db-core-e2e-tests`, `rest-client-integration-testing` — and **nothing that decides which one applies to the behaviour in front of you**. That's the single most valuable missing piece in your entire testing stack. (b) **The tautological-test anti-pattern**: "the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does, so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code." This is the most common AI-authored test failure. Your Evident Data pattern gestures at it; it doesn't *name the failure*, and naming it is what makes it catchable in review. Also worth adopting: Matt's "refactoring is not part of the loop — it belongs to review", which resolves the tension between your refactor step and `code-review` both claiming that territory. |
| **Addresses your naivety** | **Yes on content, no on integration.** The book knowledge is excellent. What's missing is the wiring: it duplicates `unit-testing`'s territory at the edges (both discuss mocking and test quality) with no single source of truth, and it doesn't route to your four integration-testing skills at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Verdict:** the best *content* of your four and of all three repos on TDD coverage. Needs enforcement teeth, a seam router, the tautological anti-pattern, and 60% of its body moved to reference files.

## 7. Cross-cutting gaps in your base

Ordered by cost of leaving them open.

1. **No elicitation layer.** Nothing in 32 skills interviews you. Both repos independently identify this as failure mode #1 and both put an interview stage first, ahead of everything else.
2. **No persistent project memory.** No glossary, no ADR convention, no on-disk spec or plan. Every session re-derives domain vocabulary from the codebase (expensive) or fetches from Jira (remote and expensive). Nothing survives a compaction.
3. **No orchestration layer.** 32 flat skills, all executing in one context window, on one model, with no controller/worker split, no ledger, no worktrees, no model tiers. This is the ceiling on both cost and capability.
4. **No router.** 32 skills is well past what a human indexes reliably. Your README table is a good *docs-side* router, but there is no in-session `ask-rob`. Matt's diagnosis is exact: piled-up cognitive load is cured by one user-invoked skill that names the others.
5. **No verification gate.** Nothing enforces evidence before completion claims. `check-diagnostics` is the right *tool* with no gate around it.
6. **Invocation hygiene.** Only `implement-issue` sets `disable-model-invocation: true`. The other 31 descriptions are permanently resident — several are enormous (`pr-comment-addresser` ~150 words; `kafka-core-and-outbox-core` ~120 plus an argument grammar; `plantuml-diagrams`' `argument-hint` is a whole DSL). Most of these are things *you* type. Per Matt's split they should cost zero context.
7. **Descriptions summarise workflow.** Several of your descriptions describe *what the skill does* in process terms (`code-review`: "Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side"; `my-skills-audit`: "Combines deterministic mechanical checks… with a semantic conflict review"). Superpowers' single most useful empirical finding is that this creates a shortcut agents take *instead of reading the body*. Their measured case: a description saying "code review between tasks" caused one review where the body specified two.
8. **No debugging discipline.** Zero of 32 skills. Every session invents its own approach to a failing Kafka consumer test.
9. **No branch lifecycle.** No worktree creation, no clean-baseline verification, no merge/PR/keep decision point, no cleanup. `pr-comment-addresser` handles post-PR feedback but nothing gets you *to* the PR.
10. **No design vocabulary.** Your standards skills say how to write a class correctly; nothing says how to decide what the class *is*, where its seam goes, or whether a port is justified. Matt's one-adapter-vs-two rule alone would prevent a lot of speculative indirection in a microservice codebase.
11. **Standards reachability.** 2,745 lines across `java-21-standards` + `java-21-springboot-standards` and their 76 reference files, reachable only via `code-review`'s `--stat` heuristic. During *implementation* — when it would actually change the code — nothing reaches them.
12. **No authoring discipline or behavioural evals.** `my-skills-audit` checks *structure* (excellently). Nothing checks *behaviour*: does the skill actually change what the agent does? Superpowers' answer is TDD-for-documentation with adversarial subagent pressure tests; Matt's is the no-op test ("does this line change behaviour versus the default?").

This is a genuinely original contribution to skill-base design.                                                   |

## 9. The roadmap

Five phases. Phase 0 is a day's work with immediate payoff; Phase 1 is the biggest correctness win; Phase 2 the biggest cost and scale win. Do not start Phase 2 before Phase 1 — a subagent execution loop fed by an un-grilled ticket just produces the wrong thing faster and more expensively.

### Phase 0 — Hygiene (1 day, no new skills)

**0.1 Invocation sweep.** Classify every skill as user-invoked or model-invoked.

- **User-invoked** (`disable-model-invocation: true`, human-facing one-line description, trigger lists stripped): `to-jira-issues`, `implement-issue`, `process-transcript`, `generate-playbooks`, `generate-manual-test-pack`, `generate-comm-manual-tests`, `create-service-configs`, `setup-mockoon-from-openapi`, `update-from-openapi`, `confluence-sync`, `confluence-reader`, `icm-architect`, `plantuml-diagrams`, `my-skills-audit`, `jacoco-test-coverage-report`, `pr-comment-addresser`.
- **Model-invoked** (keep rich triggers): `code-review`, `tdd-by-example`, `unit-testing`, `check-diagnostics`, the `*-standards` skills, `kafka-core-and-outbox-core`, `db-core`, `rest-client`, `logging-mdc-best-practices`, `resiliency-patterns-guide`, `database-access`, the three integration-testing skills.
- Move `plantuml-diagrams`' `argument-hint` grammar into the body.

**0.2 Strip workflow summaries from descriptions.** Every description states *triggering conditions only*. Delete process descriptions: "Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side", "Combines deterministic mechanical checks with a semantic conflict review", "Produces structured markdown playbooks covering deployment, rollback, …". Target: under 300 characters for model-invoked skills.

**0.3 Add explicit models to every sub-agent dispatch.** In `code-review` (both axes), and any `Explore` dispatch. Rule of thumb from Superpowers, which is nuanced enough to trust: cheapest tier only when the work is transcription with the content supplied; mid-tier as the *floor* for reviewers and for anything driven from prose; most capable for the final whole-branch review. Turn count beats token price.

**0.4 Add the review-package script.** `skills/code-review/scripts/review-package <base> <head>` writing commits + `--stat` + `git diff -U10` to one file; hand both sub-agents the path. One diff generation, zero diff in your context. (Superpowers' version is ~40 lines of bash; port it directly.)

**0.5 Add severity + verdict to `code-review` output.** `Critical (must fix) / Important (should fix) / Minor (nice to have)`, each with `file:line`, what's wrong, why it matters, how to fix; then `Ready to merge? Yes | No | With fixes` **per axis**. Keep the no-reranking rule.

---

### Phase 1 — Front of the funnel (1–2 weeks, 4 new skills)

**Status: 1.1–1.4 done, 1.5 parked.** 1.1–1.3 landed via composition instead of forking, decided after finding that `grilling`/`domain-modeling`/`to-spec` are lockfile-vendored from `mattpocock/skills` (`skills-lock.json`, installed via `npx skills experimental_install` into `.agents/skills/` → symlinked into `.claude/skills/`) rather than authored in this repo. Editing them directly would silently diverge from that hash-pinned install on the next sync, with no fork mechanism to catch it — which is exactly what had already happened once (see below). A follow-up grilling session then closed 1.3's remaining tail (self-review/gate/Confluence-publish) together with 1.4, once it became clear they were one dependency chain — see the finalized design below, which supersedes the "parked, not decided" scope note that used to sit here.

**1.1 `grilling` — done, via a sibling skill, not an edit.** `grilling` itself is untouched and still tracks upstream exactly. The stack-specific question classes live instead in a new model-invoked companion, [`domain-grilling-questions`](../../skills/domain-grilling-questions/SKILL.md), which co-fires alongside `grilling` on its own trigger keywords (kafka, outbox, avro, circuit breaker, db-core, MDC) rather than being called by it. Scope ended up broader than this section's original Kafka-only sketch: Kafka/outbox (`kafka-core-and-outbox-core`), db-core (writer/reader split, `repository.groups`, Flyway numbering, IAM lifetime), resiliency (`resiliency-patterns-guide`), and logging/MDC (`logging-mdc-best-practices`) — all four, since the question list costs nothing extra to extend once written and skipping one just defers its cost to a later review finding.

**1.2 `domain-modeling` — done, deliberately left unextended.** Stays Matt's pristine vendored original; no stack-specific content was added to it, on the same no-forking reasoning as 1.1. In the process we found `skills/domain-modeling` — a one-off local fork committed once (`6a5088e`) that had quietly diverged from the live vendored copy (different description, different reference paths) and was never wired into `.claude/skills/` at all, so every edit to it was inert. Deleted rather than repaired, since a divergent, unreachable copy served no purpose once forking was ruled out as the mechanism going forward.

The `CONTEXT.md` + ADR convention itself is **still not seeded anywhere** — that part of 1.2 remains open. This repo (`my-skills`) is the skills-authoring base, not a service repo, so there's no glossary to seed here; it happens the first time this skill set runs against a real credit-domain service.

**1.3 `to-spec` — done, also via composition, not a fork.** The seam-ladder table and `Global Constraints` section this section originally specified had already been added by directly forking Matt's `to-spec` (`skills/to-spec`) — which turned out to have the identical problem as 1.2's `domain-modeling` fork: divergent from the live vendored copy, never reachable, silently inert. That fork is deleted; `to-spec` itself is back to matching upstream exactly. In its place:

- The seam ladder now lives in a new sibling skill, [`test-seams`](../../skills/test-seams/SKILL.md) — pulled forward from Phase 3.1 (see below, now marked done) rather than bolted onto `to-spec`'s body, since a seam router is independently useful to `code-review` and `diagnosing-bugs` later and shouldn't be trapped inside one user-invoked skill. It co-fires on seam/test-plan language during `to-spec` (or anywhere else that language comes up) with no explicit call. Deliberately scoped to just the ladder table — Matt's dependency-category/adapter framework stays out until `codebase-design` itself is adopted in Phase 3, so it isn't a half-imported vocabulary.
- `Global Constraints` moved into `domain-grilling-questions` (1.1) instead of `to-spec` — it reads as a category checklist a grilling round should pin down ("state the Java/Spring Boot baseline, library versions, code style, ...") rather than testing content. It names *categories* and points at the owning domain skill's own baseline table as the source of truth rather than hardcoding version numbers — motivated by a real drift example found while doing this: `kafka-core-and-outbox-core`'s Baseline Versions table lists `db-core` at `0.0.9`, while `db-core`'s own SKILL.md is at `0.0.12`.
- **Closed in a follow-up grilling session (see 1.4 below)**: the self-review pass, hard user-approval gate, and Confluence-publishing step live in a new sibling skill, [`spec-review-and-publish`](../../skills/spec-review-and-publish/SKILL.md), co-firing after `to-spec` produces a draft — same composition discipline as `domain-grilling-questions`/`test-seams`. Confluence is now the canonical spec of record that both `to-github-issues` and `to-jira-issues` link back to.

**1.4 Split `to-jira-issues` — done.** While working through 1.1–1.3, a bigger restructuring surfaced: a **`to-jira-issues` / `to-github-issues` split**, where GitHub carries the technical spec (Mermaid diagrams, technical notes — GitHub is where the repo already lives and renders Mermaid natively) and Jira carries the business description and estimation, the two cross-referencing each other. It was parked mid-1.1–1.3 pending its own grilling session; that session happened and the design below is what got built. Matt's `to-tickets` (tracer bullets, blocking edges, expand→migrate→contract) moved into `to-github-issues`.

This is **explicitly parked, not decided** — it's a separate design tree (the GitHub/Jira ownership boundary, cross-referencing mechanics, which skill generates PlantUML and when) that needs its own grilling session before any 1.4 work should start. The original three-way split below is still a reasonable shape for the content, but its destination (one skill vs. split across two trackers) is undecided, so none of it — including the `Interfaces` block and the negation rewrite — has been started:

| New skill                | Invocation | Contents                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `to-jira-issues`         | user       | Breakdown + publish only. Tracer bullets, blocking edges, expand→migrate→contract, the user quiz, then create.                                                                                                                   |
| `evolve-jira-issue`      | user       | Evolve mode: mandatory change comment first (What changed / Motivation / Originally requested by), then the edit.                                                                                                                |
| `references/jira-mcp.md` | —          | All connector mechanics: the two-call create-then-edit ADF sequence, field discovery, "never create unless asked", "never modify the parent", "report the key and URL immediately". Reached only by the create and evolve paths. |

**Superseded — the split above is what was actually built (see the finalized design after this table), via a dedicated grilling session rather than the assumptions this table was drafted under:**

- **Re-primitived the sizing.** Lead with "demoable or verifiable on its own" + "fits one fresh context window" as the primary rule; the file-count cap is now a sanity check ("~20 files is a signal to look again, not a rule"), not the rule itself — landed in `to-github-issues`, where breakdown ownership now lives.
- **Added an `Interfaces` block per issue:** *consumes* (what earlier issues in the breakdown produce that this one needs) and *produces* (exact names/types later issues or the paired Jira ticket rely on) — Avro record + schema name, topic, consumer group, header set, DTO shape, endpoint path + method, repository group, Flyway migration number. Landed in `to-github-issues`' Task Details template.
- **Negation rewrite** was not revisited in this pass — the write guardrails (never create/modify without explicit ask) stayed as hard prohibitions, since they can't be phrased positively without weakening them.

**Finalized design (done):** a **`to-jira-issues` / [`to-github-issues`](../../skills/to-github-issues/SKILL.md) split** (both plural — single/breakdown dual-mode, matching; `evolve-*-issue` stays singular since evolve always targets one existing issue). Decisions reached, in order:

1. Target service repos' code lives on GitHub, confirming the split was worth pursuing over a Jira-only re-split.
2. Ownership boundary: **GitHub owns the entire Task Details block** (Goal, Spec Foundation, Scope, Deliverables, Acceptance Criteria, Interfaces, Verification, Notes/Risks, diagrams). **Jira owns business-only content** (title, user story, short description, estimation criteria, blockers).
3. Diagrams for GitHub use **Mermaid**, not PlantUML — GitHub renders Mermaid natively in issue bodies; PlantUML needs an external render proxy and doesn't render inline. `plantuml-diagrams` stays untouched for Confluence/business docs; a new sibling [`mermaid-diagrams`](../../skills/mermaid-diagrams/SKILL.md) covers the GitHub-bound types (sequence/state/activity).
4. `to-tickets`' tracer-bullet + blocking-edge breakdown moved into `to-github-issues`, expressed as GitHub's **native issue-dependencies API** rather than a text convention — the same mechanism `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`'s wayfinder section already documents. `to-jira-issues/references/slicing.md` moved to `to-github-issues/references/slicing.md` accordingly.
5. `to-github-issues` creates **first**. `to-jira-issues` creates second, reading the Acceptance Criteria list back out of the paired GitHub issue's Task Details and writing it to Jira's dedicated AC field (`customfield_10567`) — AC is mandatory for backlog pull, so it's no longer independently drafted in Jira.
6. **Verify-and-report gate, per pair, not per batch**: after each Jira ticket is created against its GitHub issue, both are fetched back and checked for a working mutual link before the pair is reported done — never claim a pair complete on an unverified link. Avoids orphaned pairs.
7. [`evolve-github-issue`](../../skills/evolve-github-issue/SKILL.md) (new) mirrors `evolve-jira-issue`'s mandatory-change-comment pattern; both now flag — but never auto-edit — the linked tracker/spec when a change looks like it should propagate (see Phase 1.5 below).
8. The Confluence spec page — published via a new sibling skill, [`spec-review-and-publish`](../../skills/spec-review-and-publish/SKILL.md) (closes 1.3's tail: self-review, hard approval gate, then publish) — gets a follow-up edit (`to-jira-issues` Stage 5) adding a table linking every created GitHub issue + Jira ticket back to it. It's the three-way hub: spec ↔ GitHub issue ↔ Jira issue, all cross-linked.
9. First ADR in this repo: `docs/adr/0001-github-jira-confluence-issue-split.md`.

---

### Phase 1.5 — Coordinated two-sided evolution (parked)

**Status: explicitly parked, not built.** Both `evolve-github-issue` and `evolve-jira-issue` only **flag** a linked tracker/spec as possibly stale when Acceptance Criteria, Scope, or Interfaces change — they never auto-propagate the edit to the other side. In practice, a change request often needs to update *both* the GitHub technical issue and the Jira business ticket together (e.g. a scope narrowing changes both the Interfaces block and the Estimation Criteria blast-radius sentence), and today's flag-only behaviour leaves that coordination entirely manual.

This needs its own grilling session before being built — same reasoning as why the GitHub/Jira split itself was parked mid-1.1–1.3: the design tree here (does one evolve invocation drive both trackers, or do they stay separately triggered with a stronger cross-check; does the Confluence spec ever get edited as part of an evolve; how does this interact with the verify-and-report gate) hasn't been walked yet.

---

### Phase 2 — Plan and execute (2–3 weeks, the biggest jump)

**2.1 `writing-plans`** — user-invoked, target ~120 lines. Output: `docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<BBCDA-nnnn>-<slug>.md`.

**Forward-note from the Phase 1.4 grilling session (not built yet, no Phase 2 skill exists to touch — recorded here so 2.1 isn't built on a stale assumption):** this section was designed when Jira alone carried Global Constraints/Interfaces/AC/Scope, so the template below duplicates content that now lives durably in the GitHub issue's Task Details (`to-github-issues`, Phase 1.4). When 2.1 is actually built, the plan file should **reference the paired GitHub issue by URL** instead of restating Global Constraints/Interfaces/AC/Scope, keeping only the execution-level bite-sized code steps the GitHub issue can't hold — otherwise this becomes a second, driftable source of truth for the same technical contract.

Port Superpowers' structure wholesale — it is the most thoroughly cost-optimised artifact in either repo:

- Header: Goal / Architecture / Tech Stack / **Spec URL** / `## Global Constraints` (verbatim from the spec) — *per the forward-note above, prefer linking to the paired GitHub issue over restating these once 1.4 has landed.*
- Per task: **Files** (exact paths, line ranges for modifications, test paths) → **Interfaces** (consumes / produces, exact signatures) → bite-sized steps **containing real code**.
- **No placeholders**, treated as plan failures: no "TBD", no "add appropriate error handling", no "write tests for the above", no "similar to Task N" (repeat the code — tasks are read out of order).
- Task right-sizing: fold Flyway migrations, `application.yaml` changes, and Avro `.avsc` additions into the task whose deliverable needs them.
- Self-review: spec coverage / placeholder scan / **cross-task type consistency**.

For your stack, a plan task's steps look like: write the failing `@DataJpaTest` → run it, expect FAIL with *this* message → add the entity field + Flyway `V<n>__*.sql` → run it, expect PASS → `mvn test -Dtest=<Class> 2>&1 | grep -E "Tests run|BUILD"` → commit.

**2.2 `implement-issue` v2** — the SDD controller. This is the centrepiece.

```
SETUP
  · worktree (2.3) + verified clean baseline
  · ledger at .agents/sdd/<plan-slug>/progress.md, first line names the plan
  · read the plan ONCE; note Global Constraints; one todo per task
  · pre-flight conflict scan → a TABLE in the ledger:
      one row per task-pair sharing a file, an Avro schema, a topic,
      or a Flyway migration number; one row per task on self-consistency
  · rule on every conflict found; record each Ruling

PER TASK
  1 record BASE sha; scripts/task-brief PLAN N → brief file
    dispatch implementer with EXPLICIT MODEL:
      brief path + report path + interfaces from earlier tasks +
      your rulings + Global Constraints
      never the plan file, never prior-task history
      contract: no sub-subagents, no self-dispatched reviewer
  2 status: DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
  3 scripts/review-package PLAN BASE HEAD → dispatch code-review v2
      two verdicts required: spec ✅/❌/⚠️  AND  quality Approved/Needs-fixes
  4 FIX LOOP, max 5 rounds:
      R1-3 resume the same implementer with the findings verbatim
      R4-5 fresh implementer, one model tier up
      every round ends in a SCOPED re-review of the fix diff only
      minors go to the ledger as deferred, never into the loop
      breaker at R5 → adjudicate: park with a Ruling, or rule on the
        load-bearing ones and carry the ruling into the next dispatch
  5 ledger: Task N: complete (commits a7..b7, review clean)

FINAL
  whole-branch review on the most capable model, pointed at the ledger's
  deferred-minors list; ONE fix wave; one scoped re-review; adjudicate residuals
  report "Rulings I made" — every ledger line containing Ruling:, exhaustively
  → finishing-a-development-branch (2.5)
```

Keep every token optimisation you already have, and add the ones that only work at this level: artifacts handed over as file paths (never pasted), explicit model per dispatch, batching same-shape work (e.g. "add `@Valid` to these six controllers" is one dispatch, not six), and the four-and-only-four stop conditions so the loop doesn't stall on questions you can rule on.

Port both scripts directly — `task-brief` (awk-extracts one task's text from the plan) and `review-package`. They're ~50 lines of bash each and they are what keeps the plan and the diff out of your context entirely.

**2.3 `dev-branch-setup`** — model-invoked, ~40 lines. Worktree under `.worktrees/<BBCDA-nnnn>`, branch named from the issue key, `mvn -q clean install -DskipTests` then a **verified green baseline** before any work, and never implement on `main`/`develop` without explicit consent.

**2.4 `verification-before-completion`** — model-invoked, ~60 lines. Port Superpowers' near-verbatim; the gate function and the claim→requires→not-sufficient table are its whole value. Add the Java-specific rows:

| Claim             | Requires (in this message)                                          | Not sufficient                                               |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Tests pass        | `Tests run: N, Failures: 0, Errors: 0` + `BUILD SUCCESS`            | filtered grep output from an earlier turn; "should pass now" |
| Build succeeds    | `mvn clean install` exit 0                                          | compiler clean; SonarLint clean                              |
| Style clean       | `check-diagnostics` reporting zero Checkstyle + Spotless violations | "I followed the standards"                                   |
| Coverage adequate | a JaCoCo report read after this run                                 | tests passing                                                |
| AC met            | criterion-by-criterion walk against the implementation              | tests passing                                                |
| Consumer works    | the actual consumer test asserting the observable outcome           | producer test passing                                        |

Keep the red flag on "any expression of satisfaction before verification" — it's the one that catches the failure mode in practice.

**2.5 `finishing-a-development-branch`** — user-invoked, ~50 lines. Verify tests on the tree you're about to integrate → confirm the base branch → exactly three options (merge locally / push + PR / keep) → execute → worktree cleanup with the provenance rule (only clean what's under `.worktrees/`, never `--force` on your own initiative). Hands off to `pr-comment-addresser` on option 2.

---

### Phase 3 — Depth (2–3 weeks)

**3.1 `test-seams`** — **the ladder half of this is already done, pulled forward into Phase 1.3.** [`skills/test-seams`](../../skills/test-seams/SKILL.md) exists now: the rules (highest seam that can go red, prefer existing, fewest possible, confirm with the user) and the full behaviour → seam → skill table below are live and co-fire on seam/test-plan language, including during `to-spec`.

| Behaviour under test                                                                    | Seam                                                     | Skill                             |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Pure domain logic, mapping, validation                                                  | class under test, no context                             | `unit-testing`                    |
| JPA mapping, custom finder, repository group wiring                                     | `@DataJpaTest` + Testcontainers PG                       | `db-core-jpa-integration-tests`   |
| Outbound HTTP contract, error translation, retry                                        | `@RestClientTest` + `MockRestServiceServer`, or WireMock | `rest-client-integration-testing` |
| Endpoint behaviour, consumer behaviour, circuit-breaker transitions, outbox publication | `@SpringBootTest` + EmbeddedKafka + Testcontainers       | `db-core-e2e-tests`               |

**Still open, deliberately deferred to whenever `codebase-design` (3.5) actually gets adopted:** Matt's dependency categories, mapped to your stack — **in-process** (deepen freely, no adapter) / **local-substitutable** (Testcontainers PG, EmbeddedKafka — seam stays internal, no port at the interface) / **remote-but-owned** (other credit-domain services → define a port, `RestClient` adapter for prod, in-memory adapter for test) / **true external** (mock adapter) — plus **one adapter = hypothetical seam, two = real one**. Importing this now would mean using `codebase-design`'s vocabulary (module/interface/adapter) before the rest of that vocabulary exists, which is why it was explicitly left out of the version built in Phase 1.

**3.2 `tdd-by-example` v2.** Keep all the content, restructure it.

- **SKILL.md (~70 lines):** the two rules, the loop, the four moves, the test list, refactor-only-on-green, and the enforcement teeth — an Iron Law block, a rationalization table (port Superpowers' rows; they're evaluated, yours would be guesses), the RED-evidence contract (command, failing output, why the failure was expected), the pristine-output rule, and Matt's **tautological-test** anti-pattern named explicitly.
- **references/:** `outside-in.md`, `characterization.md`, `desiderata.md`, `patterns.md`, `test-runners.md` — each reached by a named branch.
- Adopt Matt's "**refactoring belongs to review, not the loop**" to resolve the overlap with `code-review`.
- Point at `test-seams` for seam selection and at `unit-testing` for Java style; make `unit-testing` the single source of truth on mocking and delete the overlap from `tdd-by-example`.

**3.3 `diagnosing-bugs`** — model-invoked, ~90 lines. Port Matt's six phases; his framing is stronger. Rewrite the loop ladder for your stack, in order:

1. Failing test at the seam that reaches it (`@DataJpaTest` → `@SpringBootTest` → RestAssured).
2. `.http` file / curl against a locally-running service (you already have `rest-client` and `.http` conventions).
3. **Replay a captured Avro payload** through the consumer in isolation via EmbeddedKafka — for a Kafka microservice this is the highest-value loop on the list.
4. Testcontainers harness booting one service with mocked downstreams (you have Mockoon for this).
5. Differential loop: same payload through the previous release vs `HEAD`.
6. `mvn -Dtest=<Class>#<method>` bisect over commits.
7. Property/fuzz loop for "sometimes wrong output".
8. HITL bash script — last resort.

Keep the hard completion criterion (one named command you have **already run**: red-capable, deterministic, fast, agent-runnable), the minimise-until-every-element-is-load-bearing step, 3–5 ranked falsifiable hypotheses before touching anything, tagged `[DEBUG-a4f2]` logs so cleanup is one grep, and the perf branch (measure first — actuator metrics, JFR, query plan). Add Superpowers' **"3+ failed fixes ⇒ stop and question the architecture"**, which Matt's version lacks and which is the correct circuit breaker.

**3.4 `code-review` v3 — add the correctness axis.** Third parallel sub-agent, and for your stack it needs a domain checklist the other two axes structurally cannot cover:

- **Kafka/Avro:** schema change backward/forward compatible? consumer idempotent on redelivery? `Event-Type` / `Schema-Name` / `Correlation-Id` / `Causation-ID` headers set and propagated? DLQ path exists? circuit-breaker pause/resume correct?
- **Transactions/outbox:** publication inside the writer transaction or via the outbox? `writerTransactionManager` wired? any read-your-writes assumption against the reader datasource?
- **Data:** Flyway migration numbering conflict-free, forward-only, reversible-or-explicitly-not? nullable columns matching the entity?
- **Resiliency:** timeouts set on every outbound call? retry idempotent? bulkhead sized?
- **Observability:** MDC propagated across `@KafkaListener`, `@Async`, and schedulers? no PII in logs?
- **Tests:** do the new tests verify real behaviour or mock behaviour? are they tautological?

Also add: an **adversarial verification pass** (one cheap agent per finding, prompted to *refute* it; drop findings that don't survive), "**do not trust the report**", "**a stated rationale never downgrades a finding's severity**", and "**do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer**".

**3.5 `codebase-design`** — model-invoked, ~60 lines. Port Matt's glossary and principles verbatim; use the terms *exactly*. The deletion test and the one-vs-two-adapter rule are the two that will change the most decisions in a microservice codebase. Reference it from `test-seams`, `to-spec`, and `code-review`.

---

### Phase 4 — Meta (ongoing)

**4.1 `ask-rob`** — user-invoked router. Map the main flow (`grilling` → `to-spec` → `spec-review-and-publish` → `to-github-issues` → `to-jira-issues` → `writing-plans` → `implement-issue` → `code-review` → `finishing-a-development-branch`), the on-ramps (`pr-comment-addresser`, `diagnosing-bugs`, `process-transcript`, `confluence-reader`), the library/standards layer, the ops-doc layer, and the maintenance layer. Treat a stale router as a bug — Matt's phrasing is right: a router that never mentions a new skill, or still routes to a retired one, is a router that lies.

**4.2 `writing-skills` for this base.** Fold in Matt's levers as the *theory*: the two loads, the information-hierarchy ladder, progressive disclosure by **branch**, co-location, leading words, negation-as-failure-mode, the no-op test, pruning and sediment. Fold in Superpowers' *method*: description = triggering conditions only, verb-first naming, keyword coverage, and TDD-for-documentation — baseline the behaviour without the skill, note the exact rationalizations, write the skill against those, verify compliance, then hunt new loopholes.

**4.3 Extend `my-skills-audit`** with three new mechanical checks that fall straight out of this analysis:

- **C-desc-budget:** description over 300 chars, or containing workflow language ("runs", "then", "combines", "produces … covering").
- **C-invocation:** a skill you only ever type that lacks `disable-model-invocation: true`.
- **C-negation-density:** count of never / must not / do not / don't per 100 words, flagged above a threshold, with the positive-target rewrite as the recommendation.

**4.4 Phase-boundary guidance.** Write your own short version of Matt's five-option tree (continue / clear / handoff / subagent / compact, first *yes* wins, decided **at** a boundary). Put it in `ask-rob` or your top-level `CLAUDE.md`. The primary-vs-secondary-source insight — every move except Continue turns the session into a lossy summary of itself — is what makes the ordering non-obvious and worth writing down.

**4.5 Behavioural evals.** You don't need Superpowers' tmux harness. Three scripted prompts per critical skill, run against a fresh session, with a written expectation each. Examples: *"just add the field, skip the tests"* → does `tdd-by-example` v2 hold the line? *"looks good, ship it"* → does `verification-before-completion` demand evidence? *"here's BBCDA-1234, implement it"* with a deliberately ambiguous ticket → does `grilling` fire before code gets written?

### Sequencing summary

| Phase                 | Effort    | New skills                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Primary payoff                                                                                                       |
| --------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **0** Hygiene         | ~1 day    | 0                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Immediate resident-context reduction; correct model selection; one-diff reviews; actionable review verdicts          |
| **1** Front of funnel | 1–2 weeks | **Done:** `domain-grilling-questions`, `test-seams`, `spec-review-and-publish`, `to-github-issues`, `evolve-github-issue`, `mermaid-diagrams` (all composed, not forked — `grilling`/`domain-modeling`/`to-spec` stayed pristine). **Open:** `CONTEXT.md`/ADR not yet seeded in a service repo (the one in this repo covers skill-authoring vocabulary only); **1.5** coordinated two-sided evolution parked | **Correctness.** Stops building the wrong thing. `CONTEXT.md` compounds across every session thereafter, once seeded |
| **2** Plan + execute  | 2–3 weeks | 5 (`writing-plans`, `implement-issue` v2, `dev-branch-setup`, `verification-before-completion`, `finishing-a-development-branch`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | **Cost and scale.** Breaks the single-context ceiling; the 20-file cap can relax; work survives compaction           |
| **3** Depth           | 2–3 weeks | 3 new + 2 rebuilt (`test-seams`, `diagnosing-bugs`, `codebase-design`, `tdd-by-example` v2, `code-review` v3)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | **Quality.** Right tests at the right seam; root-cause discipline; the bugs your two review axes can't see           |
| **4** Meta            | ongoing   | 1 new + audit extensions (`ask-rob`, `writing-skills`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | **Compounding.** The base improves itself instead of accumulating sediment                                           |

**If you only do one thing:** Phase 1.2, `CONTEXT.md` + `domain-modeling`. It is the cheapest item on the list, it pays back in every skill you already have, and it is the one piece of either repo that its own author calls the coolest technique in the set.

**If you only do one week:** Phase 0 in full, then Phase 1.1 (`grilling`) and Phase 1.2 (`CONTEXT.md`). That's hygiene plus the two things that stop you building the wrong thing.
